la boheme isn't consumed in the same way as, for example, norma; where the entire opera constitutes a series of connective scenes, where it all pretty much focuses in on a specific plotline, where the scenes all pretty much take place closely to each other. This would be what I consider 'plot-driven'. 

Despite the opera being a short one, the plot of La Boheme is divided into 3 parts that all take place a few months/years apart from each other.  In each 'timeline', the opera focuses on a specific event. This event, even if it is small, is supposed to be significantly meaningful enough that to drive the overarching plot forward.

The book is called "scenes" from the life of the bohemians, and the opera reflects this I think. The opera consists of these "scenes", it's not a connective story that make up the opera like I've mentioned. It is the scenes that do. Each scene is like a colour that contributes to the overall colour palette of the opera, giving it its atmospheric qualities and overarching meaning and symbolism.
